lead: From today the Passion comes clearly into view. The Book of Wisdom gives the reasoning of people who cannot bear a just man and decide to test his claim that God is his Father. John shows Jesus going up to Jerusalem quietly, teaching in the Temple while people argue about where he comes from, and no one able to touch him because “his hour had not yet come”. Psalm 34 answers both: “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted.” The plot is real, but the hour belongs to God.

set: The Book of Wisdom was written in Greek by a Jewish author, very probably at Alexandria in Egypt, in the first century BC or close to it. It speaks in the name of Solomon as a literary device. Its readers were Jews living among Greek thought and pagan religion, under pressure to give up their way of life. The Catholic Church counts it among the inspired books of the Old Testament (CCC 120), as the Council of Trent reaffirmed (1546). It came down in the Greek Old Testament used by the early Church; Protestant Bibles, following the shorter Hebrew canon, leave it out or print it apart. The difference can be stated without hostility.

The speakers are “the ungodly” (1:16). In vv. 1b–11, which the reading leaves out, they set out their creed: life is short, death is the end, so let us enjoy ourselves and let might be our right. Many scholars think that some of them are Jews who have abandoned the Law, since the just man accuses them of “sins against the law” (v. 12). This is a writer warning his own community, not a judgment on any people.
str: v. 1a: the verdict: they reasoned unsoundly.
vv. 12–16: why they hate the just man: he is a living reproach.
vv. 17–20: the plan: test his claim by torture and a shameful death.
vv. 21–22: the author's comment: they did not know God's secret purposes.
kw: Pais (v. 13) means both child and servant. The same word is used for the Servant in the Greek of Isaiah 52:13, so the two ideas meet here: the just man is both God's servant and his child.

The word in v. 19, which also carries the sense of patience and fairness. Paul uses it of “the meekness and gentleness of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:1). The persecutors mean to test it by cruelty, and in the Passion it stands the test.

Literally “the mysteries of God” (v. 22). Their logic is sharp, but it leaves out what God intends. The next verse says that God created us for incorruption, and 3:1 says that “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God”.
vv: because he is inconvenient to us and opposes our actions;
It is an honest confession. They do not say he is wrong, but that he is in the way. A good life can feel like an accusation to those around it.
the very sight of him is a burden to us,
He does not need to preach. His way of living is enough. The verse describes a hatred that many just people have met, in every age.
Let us see if his words are true, and let us test what will happen at the end of his life; for if the righteous man is God’s child, he will help him,

These words come strikingly close to the mockery at the Cross: “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43). Matthew's words also recall Psalm 22:8, and the Church hears both as a preparation for the Passion.
Thus they reasoned, but they were led astray, for their wickedness blinded them,
The author does not say that God failed to help. He says that their calculation was wrong, because they could see only as far as death.
ch: St Augustine reads this passage as a prophecy of the Passion of Christ (City of God 17,20, in substance). Heard two weeks before Good Friday, it invites us to listen to the voice of those who plotted and to ask whether it is ever our own. The Church has always taught that all sinners were the authors of Christ's Passion (CCC 598), so the people of Wisdom 2 cannot be identified with any nation. And she has never drawn from this page the idea that God does not help the just: the answer to “he will help him” is Easter.

r.h: His hour had not yet come
set: The festival of Booths (Sukkot) is the great autumn pilgrim feast, when people lived in shelters of branches to remember the desert years (Leviticus 23:42–43). In Jesus' time it included rites of water and light in the Temple, and John will use these (7:37–39; 8:12). Since the sabbath healing in Jerusalem (chapter 5) Jesus has stayed in Galilee, because the authorities in Judea are seeking his death. In v. 1 the Greek Ioudaioi stands in contrast to Galilee: it refers to those in Judea who oppose him.
The reading passes over the conversation with his brothers (vv. 3–9) and his early teaching in the Temple (vv. 11–24), and picks up the dispute among the people of Jerusalem.
str: vv. 1–2: Jesus stays in Galilee; Booths is near.
v. 10: he goes up, not publicly.
vv. 25–27: the people of Jerusalem wonder, and raise an objection about his origin.
vv. 28–29: Jesus cries out in the Temple.
v. 30: they try to arrest him, and no one can.
kw: The word that governs John's Gospel. At Cana “My hour has not yet come” (2:4); here again; at 12:23 “The hour has come”. It means the Passion, death, Resurrection and return to the Father. Nobody can force it or stop it.
The verb in v. 28, used for a loud and solemn proclamation. Jesus is not secretive once he is in the Temple: he speaks so that all can hear.
vv: But after his brothers had gone to the festival, then he also went, not publicly but as it were in secret.
He goes up on his own terms and at the Father's timing. On “his brothers”, see the question below.
Yet we know where this man is from; but when the Messiah comes, no one will know where he is from.

Some Jewish writings of the time speak of the Messiah as hidden until he appears; others expected him from Bethlehem, as tomorrow's Gospel shows (7:42). John's irony is gentle: they know that he comes from Nazareth, and they do not know that he comes from the Father.
I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.
The whole of Jesus' identity is in this short verse: he knows the Father, he comes from the Father, he is sent. He answers the question of where he is from at a level his hearers had not considered.
Then they tried to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.
Danger surrounds him, yet he is not a victim of chance. When the hour comes he will give himself: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (10:18).
ch: The Church teaches that Jesus' death did not happen by chance, but belongs to the mystery of God's plan (CCC 599), and that he accepted it willingly (CCC 609). The Catechism also notes that the religious authorities in Jerusalem were not unanimous about him (CCC 596), and today's Gospel shows the same mixed picture among the people: wondering, objecting, some drawn to him. The first reading gives us the plot, and the Gospel shows who is really in charge.

qa: The Church has always understood Jesus' “brothers” as close relations, not as other children of Mary (CCC 499–501). In Hebrew and Aramaic usage “brother” could cover close kinsmen: Abram says it of his nephew Lot (Genesis 13:8, where the NRSV says “kindred”). The Gospels themselves show that James and Joseph, named among the “brothers” (Matthew 13:55), are the sons of another Mary (Matthew 27:56; CCC 500). Other Christians read these verses differently, and the Catholic understanding can be explained with respect.
study: “The very sight of him is a burden to us.” Whose goodness makes me uncomfortable? What might that discomfort be trying to teach me?
Jesus moved through real danger with trust in his Father's hour. What is in front of me that I am trying to control, instead of trusting God's timing?
